hints: Count the carbons first. Notice that 1-bromopropane has 3 carbons but butanoic acid has 4, so one carbon must be added in step X.
Recall which nucleophile adds one extra carbon to a halogenoalkane. This tells you the identity of compound Q as a nitrile.
Think about how to convert that nitrile into a carboxylic acid, and whether you need acidic or alkaline conditions to get the free acid directly.
walkthrough:
**Compare the carbon skeletons**

Look carefully at the start and finish. 1-bromopropane is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$ with 3 carbons, while butanoic acid is $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ with 4 carbons.

So reagent X must add one carbon by nucleophilic substitution.

**Identify reagent X and compound Q**

Cyanide ion, $\text{CN}^-$, is the classic reagent that adds one carbon. Heating with $\text{KCN}$ in ethanol gives a nitrile:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Br} + \text{CN}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + \text{Br}^-$$
So compound Q is butanenitrile.

**Convert the nitrile to the carboxylic acid**

Nitriles are hydrolysed by heating with dilute aqueous acid to give the free carboxylic acid directly:
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} + \text{NH}_4^+$$
That means reagent Y is $\text{HCl(aq)}$, heated under reflux. This matches X as KCN in ethanol and Y as HCl(aq).

options.A: Correct. KCN in ethanol substitutes Br with CN and extends the chain from 3 to 4 carbons to give butanenitrile. Acid hydrolysis with HCl(aq) then gives free butanoic acid.
options.B: X is correct to make the nitrile, but Y is wrong. Heating a nitrile with NaOH(aq) gives the carboxylate salt, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-$, not the free butanoic acid. You would need a further acidification step.
options.C: NH3 in ethanol converts 1-bromopropane to the amine, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$, by nucleophilic substitution. It does not add a carbon, and an amine cannot be hydrolysed by HCl(aq) to a carboxylic acid.
options.D: NaOH(aq) substitutes Br with OH to give propan-1-ol, with no extra carbon. Strong oxidation then gives propanoic acid with only 3 carbons, so you can never reach butanoic acid with 4 carbons by this route.
